projects.title: Inside the Machine: The Mathematics of Small Language Models
projects.description: An upper-division general education course in which students run small language models on their own machines and learn the probability, linear algebra, numerical precision and statistics that make them work, then measure what each run costs. Every number in the book was computed by a script in this repository.

pages.title: Syllabus
pages.description: MATH 3219, Inside the Machine. What this course is, what you will do each week, how you are graded, and what you need to bring. Written for students, not for committees.

pages.title: The Math Toolkit
pages.description: A from-zero reference for every piece of mathematical notation in Inside the Machine. Twenty short topics, from what a letter standing for a number means through sigma notation, logarithms, percentages, vectors and interval notation. Each topic defines the symbol, says how to pronounce it, and works arithmetic you can reproduce on a phone calculator.

pages.title: Module A: A model is a measurable object
Where is this running, and what did it cost?
pages.description: The first session of Inside the Machine. A language model is opened as a folder of files on a disk, run on the machine in front of you, and measured twice: did it work, and what did it cost. Byte counts, gigabytes, tokens per second and joules per token are built from nothing, each with a full symbol table and worked arithmetic. Lab 0 is specified here.

pages.title: Numbers all the way down: tokens
pages.description: Chapter 2 of MATH 3219. A language model cannot read letters, so your text is cut into pieces called tokens and each piece is swapped for a whole number. Bakersfield becomes three pieces. Every digit of 1234567 becomes a token of its own, which is the measured starting point for why arithmetic is hard for them. Six formulas, each defined symbol by symbol, with arithmetic you can check on a phone.

pages.title: 3. What is a parameter?
pages.description: A parameter is one number. This chapter opens a real 494,032,768-parameter model, counts every number in it, sorts those numbers into the parts of the machine they belong to, prints one real 896 by 896 weight matrix and describes it with a mean, a standard deviation and a median, then turns the parameter count into a file size in gigabytes. The surprise is the inventory: attention, the famous part, is 8.92 per cent of this model, while a lookup table for words is 27.56 per cent. Every number was computed by lab/ch03_parameter_anatomy.py, apart from a few that name their own source file on the page.

pages.title: Module B: The probability of the next word
The probability of the next word
pages.description: The keystone chapter. A language model does not pick a word; it gives a score to every one of the 151,936 words in its dictionary. Softmax is the function that turns those scores into probabilities. This chapter builds softmax from nothing, does it by hand on the three small scores 2, 1 and 0, then runs it on the real model, where the prompt The capital of France is gives Paris 30.219 per cent and gives a fill-in-the-blank line 12.315 per cent.

pages.title: Temperature, and what it does not do
pages.description: Temperature is one division carried out on the model's scores before they become probabilities. It flattens the picture or it sharpens the picture, and it can never change which token the model ranked first. This chapter builds that claim from arithmetic you can do on a phone, measures it on a real 494,032,768-parameter model, and takes apart the sentence 'temperature makes the model more creative'.

pages.title: Bits, precision, and rounding
pages.description: Where a model's gigabytes come from, and why storing a number with fewer bits means rounding it. Bits, levels, the gap between the levels, and the error that gap creates. Chapter 6 of MATH 3219 at CSU Bakersfield.

pages.title: Quantization: what you lose, what it buys
pages.description: How a language model is made smaller by rounding every weight to a short list of allowed values. One scale for a whole matrix fails, because a single outlier weight sets the scale and an ordinary weight collapses to zero; one scale for every 32 weights fixes it. Then the measured cost of a token in joules, the measured memory each model needs, and the point where the sustainability argument and the access argument turn out to be the same argument. Every number was computed by a script in this repository.

pages.title: A sentence is an arrow
pages.short_title: Ch 8. A sentence is an arrow
pages.description: Coordinates from nothing, the length of an arrow by Pythagoras, and the dot product worked out by hand on vectors you can draw. Then the same two formulas applied without change to a real 384-number sentence vector from all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a model of 22,713,216 parameters. Every printed number comes from a JSON file in lab/out/.

pages.title: Similarity is geometry
pages.description: Cosine similarity from nothing. Why the dot product alone gets the answer wrong, what dividing by both lengths fixes, and the one line that settles it: the arrow (3, 4) and the arrow (6, 8) have a cosine of exactly 1.0000, because the second is the first doubled. Then the same measure in 384 dimensions on six real sentences, where two sentences about Bakersfield and Kern County score 0.8333, a cat and a kitten score 0.6124 while sharing no content words, and the stock market against photosynthesis goes negative. Closes on experimental control: changing one thing at a time.

pages.title: Retrieval: the open-book exam
pages.description: Chapter 10 of MATH 3219. Retrieval is nearest-neighbour search in a space of meaning. One measured query separates two relevant sentences from four irrelevant ones by a drop of 0.630, and that drop, not the top score, is the idea. Then three honest passes at a harder corpus, CSUB's own GE Compendium, ending in the result that matters: the system that answered 6 of 6 had a smaller confidence gap than the system that answered 3 of 6.

pages.title: Module E: Judging models like a statistician
Can a model take a test?
pages.short_title: 11. Can a model take a test?
pages.description: Chapter 11 of MATH 3219. Builds the idea of a proportion from nothing, separates proportions from decimals from percentages, shows why chance on a four-option question is exactly 25 percent, explains how an answer is pulled out of a model, and then reads a measured size ladder of three Qwen2.5 models on one twenty-question bank, where the number of parameters is the only thing allowed to change.

pages.title: Is that score real?
pages.description: A benchmark score is one draw, not a fact. This chapter builds the standard error, the Wald interval, the Wilson interval and the bootstrap from zero arithmetic, on the real 20-question run in which Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct scored 5 out of 20. It shows the textbook interval producing an accuracy above 100 percent, shows what statisticians use instead, and ends with the number of questions an honest benchmark needs.

pages.title: Measure your measurement
pages.description: The keystone chapter of Inside the Machine. The same small language model, answering the same twenty questions, scores 25.0%, 35.0% or 15.0% depending only on the rule used to mark it. This chapter diagnoses why, fixes it twice, shows that position bias is a symptom of a weak model, compares two models the honest paired way, and then runs McNemar's exact test on a twenty-five point gap and finds p = 0.0625, which does not clear 0.05. Every measured number was computed in the course lab, the few invented ones say so, and every formula is given in six parts.

pages.title: Bias in the benchmark, and who pays
pages.description: One overall benchmark score of 25 percent, cut into nine topics, runs from 0 percent to 100 percent. This chapter shows how to cut a score into subgroups, then shows why almost none of those subgroup numbers mean anything when each one rests on one to four questions. It closes the course's sustainability thread by putting a measured energy figure and a measured memory figure on the same three models, and asking who pays each one.

pages.title: Capstone
pages.description: The capstone specification for MATH 3219. How to pose a question about a small language model that can actually be answered, how to run the evaluation honestly, how to report the result with an interval and a resource-cost accounting, the five milestones across the semester, the 200-point rubric with its weights, the lightning-talk format, and a checklist to run against your own draft before you submit it.

pages.title: Formula Sheet
pages.description: One page holding every formula the course uses, from softmax to McNemar's exact test. Each entry says in plain English what the formula does, shows the formula, defines every symbol including the operators, reads the whole thing out loud as one sentence, works a small numeric instance with every step shown, and tells you how to check your answer.

pages.title: The Python Reference
pages.description: A from-zero reference for every piece of Python in Inside the Machine, organised by what you are trying to do rather than by language feature. Installing the tools, loading a model, tokenizing text, reading logits, softmax, temperature, top k, sentence embeddings, normalising a vector, a cosine similarity matrix, scoring a multiple-choice question by log-probability, the bootstrap, and charts in the Okabe-Ito palette. Every snippet was run on the course machine and its printed output is the real output.

pages.title: The Shelf
pages.description: The reference shelf for the course. Each model with its exact repository name, its parameter count, its size in bytes, its licence and the chapters that use it; the twenty-question bank in full, with an honest account of why twenty is too few; every JSON result file with the script that wrote it; and the reproducibility contract that says what will come back the same and what will not.

pages.title: The Cost Model
pages.description: The measured energy, speed and memory cost of the three course models, the limits of that measurement, the join that makes the sustainability argument quantitative, and the three costs this course refuses to print because it did not compute them.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.description: Plain-language definitions of every technical term in Inside the Machine, each with the chapter where it is introduced, a small concrete example drawn from the book's own measurements, and a note wherever the term is commonly misused.

pages.title: Answers
pages.description: Answers and worked solutions to the odd-numbered practice problems, chapter by chapter. Every odd-numbered problem in all fifteen chapters is worked in full, with every arithmetic step shown.
